beats.narration_text: Nearly every marketing agency now uses AI. So does most of the industry. And yet the pages that actually rank aren't the ones a machine wrote alone. This is a story about restructuring — not replacement.

show.event: Cream page, spark, serif greeting 'Kumusta, Yatra' above the composer
The ask types itself in
Terracotta send arms — the ONE accent
Three result lines stagger in — the ask lands ANSWERED

props.command: I run an agency. Everyone I compete with is using AI for SEO and content now. Show me what actually changed structurally — adoption, spend, what search rewards — and tell me honestly whether this is replacement or reorganisation.
output: agencies adopted faster than in-house teams
spend is still accelerating, not plateauing
assisted content is the norm; fully automated is rare

beats.narration_text: Hi, I'm Yatra, and this video is about how marketing agencies are restructuring around AI-driven SEO and content. The short version: adoption is nearly total, spending is still climbing, and AI-assisted writing now shows up even at the top of search results — but content written purely by machine, with nobody checking, is still rare. Stay with me and you'll see where the work actually moved.

show.event: One track labelled 'the agency workflow' holds, then splits
'Producing the draft' dives in ink
'Deciding what ships' climbs in terracotta — the ONE accent
The gap holds ≥2s — the whole episode lives in it

beats.narration_text: Act one. The adoption gap — and who moved first.

show.event: Act number types in small above the rule
Title Case serif act title draws in beneath a terracotta hairline
Holds — the viewer always knows where they are in the episode

beats.narration_text: Start with who moved first. Ninety percent of agency marketers report using AI. For in-house teams, it's eighty-one percent. Both numbers are high — but the gap runs in one direction, and it's the agencies that are ahead.

show.event: Two labelled bars grow to their values as each is spoken
The agency bar lands longer, in terracotta — the ONE accent
Source line types in beneath: Fractl, 2026
Both bars held side-by-side ≥2s

data.title: Agency vs in-house adoption
data.note: both high — the gap runs one way

beats.narration_text: That gap makes structural sense. An agency runs the same workflow across many clients, so tooling pays back faster. It sells hours, so anything that compresses hours hits the margin directly. And it competes on turnaround in a way most in-house teams simply don't.

show.event: Three reasons draw in one at a time, each on its spoken phrase
Each reason's one-line consequence types beneath it
Closing caution lands and holds ≥2s

data.slideMeta: Why the agency side moved first
data.title: Three structural reasons

items.label: The workflow repeats across clients
items.why: Tooling amortises over many accounts, not one.

items.label: The product is hours
items.why: Compressing hours hits the margin directly.

items.label: Turnaround is the pitch
items.why: Speed is competitive, not just convenient.

data.closer: No claim here about which is better — only about which had more reason to move.

beats.narration_text: One caution before we go further. Using AI covers an enormous range — from a tool that suggests keywords to a system that drafts a whole page. A single adoption number flattens all of that into one word. Keep that in mind as the numbers get bigger.

show.event: Three bands of behaviour draw in, widening in scope
Each band's note types in
The caution lands and holds ≥2s

data.title: One word, many behaviours

items.label: Outlining and briefing
items.why: Shapes the work without writing it.

data.closer: Adoption figures count all three the same. That matters later.

beats.narration_text: Act two. The money is still moving — and it isn't slowing down.

show.event: Act number types in small above the rule
Title Case serif act title draws in beneath a terracotta hairline
Holds — the viewer always knows where they are in the episode

beats.narration_text: Here are the numbers that say this isn't a plateau. Ninety-eight percent of marketers plan to increase what they spend on AI for search this year. And ninety-four percent plan to use AI in content creation itself — the writing, not just the research around it.

show.event: Two bars grow to their values as each is spoken
The spend bar lands in terracotta — the ONE accent
Source line types in: Typeface, 2026
Held ≥2s

data.title: Spend, and where it goes

items.label: Plan to increase AI SEO spend
Plan to use AI in content creation

data.note: the budget question is already settled

beats.narration_text: This is the fastest-moving number in the whole story. Two years ago, sixty-five percent of marketers were not using AI for blog writing. Today that holdout group is five percent. That isn't a decline. That's a collapse.

show.event: The 'before' bar draws at full height, labelled
On the spoken 'five percent', the bar collapses to the 'after' height in terracotta
Source line types in: Typeface, 2026
Both states held side-by-side ≥2s

data.slideMeta: Marketers NOT using AI for blog writing
data.title: From majority to rounding error

beats.narration_text: Which creates a problem nobody put in a budget. When a capability becomes nearly universal, it stops being an advantage and becomes a floor. Everyone gets faster at the same time, so speed stops distinguishing anyone. The differentiator has to move somewhere else.

show.event: A centre rule draws; two column headings type in
Left column fills in ink as each is named
Right column fills in terracotta
Footer lands and holds ≥2s

data.title: Advantage becomes floor

left.heading: When few had it
items: Tooling was a story to sell

right.heading: Now that nearly all have it
items: The story has to be about judgement

data.note: a capability everyone has is a floor, not an edge

beats.narration_text: Act three. What search actually rewards — and what it doesn't.

show.event: Act number types in small above the rule
Title Case serif act title draws in beneath a terracotta hairline
Holds — the viewer always knows where they are in the episode

beats.narration_text: So I asked Claude to separate two things people constantly conflate: pages that used AI at all, and pages that were written entirely by it.

show.event: Composer framed; spark line reads 'Some, or only?'
The prompt types itself in — the ACTUAL prompt behind the next beat
Terracotta send arms; runningText 'separating…' — cut to RESULT

props.command: Separate two things for me, because people keep merging them: the share of web pages that contain SOME AI-generated content, and the share that are PURELY AI-written with no human editing. Then tell me which of those two actually correlates with ranking.

beats.narration_text: And the split is stark. Seventy-four point two percent of new web pages contain some AI-generated content. But pages that are purely AI-written, with no human in the loop, are only two point five percent of pages.

show.event: A wide band fills to represent pages containing some AI content
A much smaller nested band lights in terracotta — purely AI-written
Source line types in: Ahrefs via Stacc, 2026
The size difference held ≥2s — it is the point of the beat

data.slideMeta: New web pages · some AI vs purely AI
data.title: 'Some' is common. 'Only' is not.
data.note: the same page can be assisted without being automated

beats.narration_text: Now take that up to the pages that actually win. Eighty-six point five percent of top-ranking search pages contain some AI-generated text. Assistance is not a penalty. It is already what the winning pages look like.

show.event: The figure counts up and settles, oversized on the cream stage
The label types in beneath it
Terracotta rule draws under the figure — the ONE accent
Source line types in: Ahrefs via Stacc, 2026. Held ≥2s

data.title: Assistance is not a penalty
data.label: of top-ranking search pages contain some AI-generated text
data.note: already what the winning pages look like

beats.narration_text: Put those two together and you get the finding that matters. Nearly everything at the top of search used AI somewhere. Almost nothing at the top of search was left entirely to it. Assisted is the norm. Automated is the exception.

show.event: Centre rule draws; two headings type in
Left column fills in ink — the norm
Right column fills in terracotta — the exception
Footer lands and holds ≥2s

data.title: Assisted is normal. Automated is rare.

left.heading: The norm
items: AI used somewhere in the process

right.heading: The exception
items: Written start to finish by machine

data.note: the distinction people keep collapsing is the whole story

beats.narration_text: Act four. What actually got restructured — and what it cost.

show.event: Act number types in small above the rule
Title Case serif act title draws in beneath a terracotta hairline
Holds — the viewer always knows where they are in the episode

beats.narration_text: Here is the part that surprises people. Seventy percent of agencies raised their prices across twenty twenty-four and twenty twenty-five — partly to cover investment in AI tooling. The efficiency gain did not arrive as a discount.

show.event: The figure counts up and settles
The label types in beneath
Terracotta rule draws under the figure
Source line types in: Backlinko/QuickSEO, 2026. Held ≥2s

data.title: The gain did not arrive as a discount
data.label: of agencies raised prices across 2024–2025, partly due to AI tooling investment
data.note: efficiency was reinvested, not passed on

beats.narration_text: So what did the money buy? Not fewer people — a different shape. Drafting compressed. Research compressed. What expanded was everything around the draft: the brief, the verification, the editing pass, and somebody accountable for what finally ships.

show.event: Four bands draw in, each landing on its spoken phrase
Each band's one-line why types in
The closer lands and holds ≥2s

data.title: The work moved around the draft

items.label: The brief
items.why: Worth more when generation is cheap.

items.label: Verification
items.why: Someone has to check what the model asserted.

items.label: Accountability
items.why: A name attached to what ships.

data.closer: Fewer hours drafting. More hours deciding.

beats.narration_text: Which shows up in who agencies hire. Roles defined by producing volume are under pressure. Roles defined by judgement — strategy, editing, subject expertise, quality control — are the ones being added. Same output, redistributed labour.

show.event: Centre rule draws; headings type in
Left column fills in ink
Right column fills in terracotta
Footer lands and holds ≥2s

beats.narration_text: And here is where this model could be wrong. It assumes search keeps rewarding assisted content. If ranking systems start penalising AI text directly, or if the purely-automated share climbs out of the low single digits, then the restructuring story becomes a replacement story. Watch that one number.

show.event: Two conditions draw in, each with a terracotta marker
Each condition's consequence types in beneath
The closing status lands and holds ≥2s

data.slideMeta: Where this breaks · the test that would falsify it
data.title: Two things that would change the answer

items.label: Ranking systems penalise AI text directly
items.why: Then assistance stops being safe, and the workflow inverts again.

items.label: The purely-automated share climbs
items.why: It sits in the low single digits today. If it stops being rare, this stops being restructuring.

data.closer: Both are observable. Neither has happened yet.

beats.narration_text: Every number in this video comes from four published sources, listed on screen now. I have not estimated anything. Where I did not have data, I said so in words instead of inventing a figure.

beats.narration_text: So, the verdict. One — agencies adopted faster than in-house teams, and they are the leading indicator for everyone else. Two — spend is still increasing, and non-use has collapsed to a rounding error. Three — assisted content is what ranks, while fully automated content stays rare. This is a restructuring of workflow, not a replacement of people. So far.

show.event: Claude artifact page opens
Four lines stagger in, one per spoken clause
The 'so far' qualifier lands last and holds

artifactLines: Agencies adopted faster than in-house teams (90% vs 81% — Fractl, 2026) and lead the change.
Spend is still rising (98% plan to increase AI SEO spend — Typeface, 2026); non-use collapsed 65% → 5%.
Assisted content is what ranks: 86.5% of top pages contain some AI text — but only 2.5% of pages are purely AI (Ahrefs via Stacc, 2026).
Restructuring, not replacement — so far. If the purely-automated share climbs, that conclusion changes.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this: audit my last ten pieces of content and tell me, for each one, which parts AI produced and which parts a person actually decided — then tell me what a reader would notice if the human half disappeared. Grade the answer on whether it separates producing from deciding, and whether it names something you would be embarrassed to publish.
